text:
A fleeting altered-state visual phenomenon may have been converted into a stationary, coordinate-addressable target.

That is genuinely interesting.

But the current draft moves too quickly from a tool Goler says has been built to results that have supposedly already been established. In the source interview, Goler describes the Apple Vision Pro software, the frozen image, the six-symbol interface and the proposed brain-recording synchronization. Crucially, he also says the decisive question—whether different people report the same symbols in the same locations—has not yet been answered.

The central framing should therefore not be:

Apple Vision Pro revealed the static code of reality.

It should be:

Apple Vision Pro may have turned an alleged DMT visual phenomenon into something science can finally address by coordinate.

Or, more memorably:

The experiment did not photograph the code. It may have built a ruler for the hallucination.

Or:

They may have frozen the canvas, not the code.

That distinction preserves the wonder while making the piece much harder to dismiss.

The strongest defensible thesis

The most compelling version of the story is not metaphysical. It is methodological:

Danny Goler says a high-resolution photograph of the laser pattern can evoke stationary, code-like forms when viewed under DMT in Apple Vision Pro. If that report survives blinded testing, the breakthrough would be a reproducible altered-state percept whose apparent location can be measured, transformed and compared across participants.

That would be scientifically valuable even if no hidden language, simulation code or external intelligence were involved.

A pixel-addressable altered-state percept could become a tool for studying:

How psychedelics alter visual inference.
How ambiguous texture becomes symbolic form.
Whether hallucinated content can be anchored to external stimuli.
Whether different brains impose similar structures on the same visual noise.
Whether the percept is locked to the image, retina, visual field or surrounding world.
Whether reports contain stimulus-specific information that generalizes to new participants.

DMT is already known to produce major changes in brain dynamics, including altered connectivity and cortical activity resembling aspects of visual stimulation even with eyes closed. Meanwhile, geometric “form constants” such as lattices, tunnels, spirals and cobweb-like structures have long been modeled as consequences of shared visual-cortical architecture. That makes a shared neural response to a highly structured texture a serious alternative to hidden external code—not a dismissive afterthought.

Claim-by-claim surgery
1. “If you use Apple Vision Pro and viewed while on DMT…”
The grammar is awkward, and the construction implies a universal effect.
Goler himself says approximately 30 per cent of people have difficulty seeing the broader laser phenomenon or do not see it at all.
Better:
Danny Goler says that some participants viewing a high-resolution image of his laser pattern in Apple Vision Pro while under DMT report seeing stationary, code-like forms.
More viral:
Danny Goler says Apple Vision Pro can freeze a DMT visual phenomenon that normally appears to move.
Most precise:
Goler reports that a still photograph of the laser pattern can act as a stationary visual scaffold for the code-like forms some participants perceive under DMT.
The word scaffold is exceptionally useful because it leaves open whether the forms are in the image, generated by the brain or produced by an interaction between them.

2. “The static symbolic code of reality becomes visible”

This sentence turns four unproved interpretations into one apparent observation:

That the marks are objectively present.

That they are symbols.

That they constitute code.

That the code belongs to reality itself.

Only the first-order report is currently supported:

Some participants reportedly perceive stationary forms that resemble characters or symbols.

Use code-like, not code, until the reports demonstrate syntax, information content or semantics.

A useful hierarchy is:

Mark.

Repeated shape.
Glyph-like form.
Stable glyph category.
Alphabet.

Syntax.

Message.

Executable code.

Fundamental code of reality.

The current claim begins near step two or three and rhetorically jumps to step nine.
A powerful corrective line:
A glyph is not a message. A message is not a program. A program is not the substrate of reality.
3. “Researchers captured a high-resolution image…”
Use:
Goler says his team captured a high-resolution image…
“Researchers” can unintentionally imply that an independent university laboratory, clinical team or established research institute performed and validated the work.
Goler credits collaborators with helping develop the Vision Pro tools, but the public source is still Goler describing his own project.
That does not diminish the engineering. It simply keeps institutional authority from being smuggled into the sentence.

4. “A high-resolution image of the laser band”

This needs a full chain of custody.

The piece should ask:

Was the source captured as RAW, TIFF, PNG or JPEG?

What camera and sensor were used?

What lens, aperture and focus distance?

What exposure and ISO?

Was sharpening applied?

Was denoising applied?

Was the image demosaiced from a Bayer sensor?

Was it resized?

Was it compressed?

Was it shown identically to both eyes?
Was it mapped to a flat virtual plane or a curved spatial surface?
What was its angular size?
What brightness and contrast were used?
Did visionOS perform dynamic resampling?
Was the image displayed at native pixel resolution?
Was the same exact file used for every participant?
Has its cryptographic hash been published?
These details are not clerical trivia. They determine whether the reported forms could be driven by:
Laser speckle.
Camera noise.
Demosaicing patterns.
Sharpening halos.
JPEG blocks.
Aliasing.
Moiré.
Micro-OLED subpixel structure.

Headset optics.

Rescaling.
Gaze-contingent rendering.
Ordinary high-contrast texture.
The image itself must become a registered scientific stimulus, not merely “the photograph.”
5. The most important optics correction
Goler says in the interview that a camera “only registers amplitude.” The technically cleaner formulation is:
A conventional camera measures optical intensity over its exposure; it does not directly preserve the original complex optical field, including phase.
In simplified form:
I(x,y)≈∫∣E(x,y,t)∣2 dtI(x,y)\approx \int |E(x,y,t)|^2\,dtI(x,y)≈∫∣E(x,y,t)∣2dt
The camera stores I(x,y)I(x,y)I(x,y), the intensity map. It does not store the complete field EEE, with its original phase relationships, unless a specialized holographic or interferometric method is used.
Laser speckle itself is a real physical intensity pattern produced by interference when coherent light scatters from a rough surface. But after that speckle pattern is photographed and displayed on a headset, the viewer is seeing a newly emitted pixel image—not the original laser wavefront.
This radically changes the central question.

The still-image result, if replicated, would not initially suggest:

Information has survived inside the original light field.

It would suggest:

A fixed two-dimensional intensity texture is sufficient to support the reported percept.

That narrows the mechanism toward some interaction among:

Recorded image statistics.
Display characteristics.
Eye optics.

DMT-altered visual processing.

Attention and expectation.

The still-image result may therefore be evidence against the necessity of live coherent light, not evidence that the complete original light field has been preserved.

A devastatingly concise line:

The photograph cannot freeze the original light field. It can only freeze the pattern the camera extracted from it.

6. “The static code remains frozen instead of running”

This is intriguing, but not inherently surprising under a stimulus-anchoring explanation.

If the moving percept was driven by a changing live speckle pattern, eye movement, viewpoint changes or dynamic visual inference, then freezing the stimulus could naturally freeze the apparent forms anchored to it.

That yields at least three interpretations:
External-code interpretation
The photograph contains a stable hidden symbolic structure that DMT reveals.
Stimulus-locked pareidolia interpretation
The photograph is a fixed high-dimensional texture. Under DMT, the visual system interprets its stable features as glyphs, so the resulting percept remains fixed.

Display-pipeline interpretation

The photograph interacts with resampling, microdisplay pixels, optical distortion or gaze-dependent rendering to create repeatable patterns that become unusually salient under DMT.

The line should therefore be:

The frozen percept suggests that the reported forms may be anchored to a reproducible visual stimulus. It does not yet establish what generates them.

Or:

The experiment may have frozen the canvas rather than captured the writing.

7. “The code only appears meaningful in the altered state”

Meaningful is doing too much work.

A shape can resemble writing without carrying meaning. Human beings readily perceive writing-like structure in bark, clouds, marble, static and damaged signage.

To demonstrate meaning, researchers would need at least one of the following:

Participants repeatedly read the same sequence.

Different participants independently transcribe the same sequence.

Symbol transitions follow stable grammatical constraints.

A symbol predicts a known external variable.

Participants recover hidden information placed into an unseen stimulus.

A symbol system permits communication or decoding.

A translation rule learned on one set generalizes to new examples.

Until then:

The image reportedly evokes structured, character-like forms under DMT.

Not:

The image contains meaningful code.

A particularly useful line:
Resembling language is a perceptual result. Carrying language is an information-theoretic result.
8. “The brain is scanned, registering exact brain events”
This is the most technically inflated line in the draft.
Apple Vision Pro contains cameras, eye tracking, hand tracking, LiDAR and motion sensors. Its published specification does not include EEG, fNIRS, MEG, fMRI or another neural-recording modality. Any “brain scan” must therefore be supplied by external equipment.
The piece needs answers to:
What neural modality is being used?

EEG?

Functional near-infrared spectroscopy?

Another wearable?

Is the device validated for research?

What is its sampling rate?

How are the clocks synchronized?

Is the neural recording continuous?

What event marker is sent when the participant selects a location?

Is the marker generated on the headset or receiving computer?

What is the synchronization error?

Is the reported “brain event” the perception, decision, menu appearance or motor response?
A click does not identify the moment a symbol first became visible. It identifies the moment the participant finished:
Perceiving something.
Deciding it was reportable.
Locating it.
Initiating a selection.
Completing the gesture.
EEG can offer high temporal resolution but has limited spatial localization; fMRI offers much stronger spatial information but relies on a slower hemodynamic response. Calling either one an “exact snapshot” without specifying the modality and model is misleading.
Better:
Goler says the app can time-stamp a participant’s selection so it can be synchronized with external neural recordings.
Even better:
The system is intended to link a reported image coordinate with the participant’s concurrent neural state, although the public description does not yet specify the imaging modality or results.

9. The motor-control problem

DMT can profoundly alter attention, time perception, coordination and task comprehension. A participant clicking slightly away from a symbol may reflect motor error rather than visual disagreement.
The experiment therefore needs a sober and altered-state calibration task:
Present ordinary visible targets.
Ask participants to select them.
Measure coordinate error.

Measure response delay.

Measure missed selections.

Measure whether error increases with eccentricity.

Estimate each participant’s uncertainty radius.

Every symbol report should be stored not as a perfect point, but as a probability distribution:

p(x,y∣participant, state)p(x,y \mid \text{participant, state})p(x,y∣participant, state)

Without that calibration, “same coordinate” may be either too strict or artificially generous.

A strong line:

Before measuring whether two minds agree, measure how accurately each altered participant can point.
10. The six-symbol radial menu may manufacture agreement
This is one of the biggest hidden design flaws.
A six-choice menu does not merely record perception. It teaches participants the project’s preferred alphabet.
It creates:
Anchoring.
Forced categorization.

Base-rate distortion.

Memory contamination.

Repeated exposure to the same forms.

Circularity if the six symbols were derived from the same participants used to validate them.

False agreement when distinct shapes are pushed into the nearest available category.

The correct sequence is:

Participant marks the location.

Participant freely traces or draws what was seen.

Participant gives a confidence rating.

Participant can select “no stable form.”
Only after the free response is locked may a forced-choice menu appear.
The menu must include “other,” “uncertain” and “none.”
Its positions must be randomized.
The symbol vocabulary must be derived from a separate discovery cohort.
It must then be tested in an untouched validation cohort.
Better wording:

The prototype includes a radial menu of six recurring glyph categories, but a rigorous study would need free-form reports first to ensure the menu is not shaping the phenomenon it is intended to measure.

A memorable line:
The measuring instrument must not teach the witness what to see.
11. “It will build a Rosetta Stone”
This metaphor is attractive but wrong.
The Rosetta Stone contained parallel versions of the same text in known and partially unknown writing systems. It supplied a translation key.
Here, there is no known reference message.
What the system might initially create is:
A coordinate-indexed phenomenology atlas.
A cross-participant glyph-concordance map.

A spatial catalog of altered-state reports.

A stimulus–perception correspondence database.

Use:

The system could build a coordinate-indexed atlas of where participants report recurring forms.

Reserve Rosetta Stone until there is an actual mapping between unknown glyphs and independently known content.

12. “AI is cataloging thousands of independent replications”

This combines three different claims:

AI involvement

Veilbreak provides an API and an MCP endpoint through which AI systems can query approved public records. That is real. Its public GitHub organization, however, currently shows no public repositories, so the underlying app and analysis pipeline are not yet openly inspectable there.

Thousands
Goler says thousands have attempted the wider phenomenon, and his exploratory report states n>1000n>1000n>1000. But that report does not supply a participant-level table, recruitment flow, standardized denominator, raw reports or statistical analysis. Its collection method is described as post-session written and verbal accounts, while controlled recurrence studies and brain imaging are listed as future work.
Independent replications
The public Veilbreak dashboard listed 57 experiment records, 37 marked as having observed the phenomenon, when checked on July 10, 2026. The entries include anonymous reports and varying substances and conditions; that is an exploratory repository, not 57 preregistered independent replications.

Use:

Veilbreak is beginning to collect public reports and expose approved records through an open read-only interface. Goler separately says thousands have attempted the broader laser experiment, but the publicly inspectable database remains much smaller and is not yet a controlled replication registry.

That is both accurate and still impressive.

13. “People worldwide who have never spoken to each other”

Never speaking is not the same as being informationally independent.

Participants may still have encountered:

Goler’s videos.

The phrase “code of reality.”

Illustrations of Katakana-like marks.

The same podcast clips.

The same online instructions.

The same six-symbol interface.

Comments from previous participants.

The claim that the forms move or resemble writing.

This is memetic contamination.

True evidential independence requires:

No prior exposure to the expected result.

Neutral instructions.
Separate recruitment channels.
Separate investigators.
Separate laboratories.
Locked protocols and outcomes.
No access to previous reports.
Publication of failures.
A held-out stimulus set.

A valuable distinction:

Social independence means participants never met. Evidential independence means their expectations and data-generating processes were not inherited from the same source.

The false dichotomy in the current ending
The draft asks:
Is information actually present in the light field itself, or is it still a projection?
Those are not the only possibilities.
There is a full causal chain:
Laser emission.
Diffraction element.
Reflective or scattering surface.
Objective speckle structure.

Camera optics.

Sensor pixel array.

Demosaicing and image processing.

Compression and resizing.

Vision Pro display pixels.

Headset lenses.

Binocular presentation.

Eye optics.
Retinal sampling.
DMT-altered cortical dynamics.
Attention and expectation.
Response interface.
AI categorization.
The scientific task is not to choose prematurely between “external code” and “internal projection.”
It is to determine:
At which layer does the reproducible structure enter the system?
This is the genius-level reframing.
The possible answers include:
The original optical stimulus.
The photographed intensity texture.
Camera artifacts.
Headset display artifacts.
Shared retinal or cortical processing.
Cultural symbol priors.

Task expectations.

Some interaction among several layers.

An unknown mechanism.

A stronger closing question:

Does the percept follow the original optical field, the stored pixels, the display, the retina, the room—or the participant’s expectation?

The three-coordinate-frame experiment
This is probably the single most elegant test the project could perform.
Every reported glyph can potentially be anchored to one of three coordinate systems.
Image coordinates
The symbol follows the image pixels.
Test:
Move the image.
Rotate it.
Mirror it.

Crop it.

Scale it.

If the symbol moves and transforms with the image, it is stimulus-locked.

That would be scientifically interesting, but still consistent with ordinary stimulus-driven pareidolia under an altered state.

Retinal or visual-field coordinates

The symbol remains in the same place relative to the participant’s gaze or visual field even when the image moves.

Test:

Shift fixation.

Present the image to one eye at a time.
Move the image while holding gaze stable.
Change head position.
Repeat after recalibration.
That would suggest a contribution from the eye or retinotopic visual system.

World coordinates

The symbol appears to stay in the same place in the surrounding room even when the image moves.

That would suggest world-centered spatial representation, memory or headset anchoring. It would be unusual, but it still would not by itself prove an external object.

A perfect line for the article:

Move the picture. Move the eyes. Move the room. The symbol’s loyalty will reveal where the phenomenon lives.

The actual ladder of proof
The current draft treats all stages as one discovery. They must be separated.
Level 1: Phenomenology
Some people say they perceive code-like shapes.
Level 2: Within-session stability

A person says the same shape remains in one place during a session.

Level 3: Within-person repeatability

The same person returns on another occasion and reports the same shape at the same location.

Level 4: Cross-person spatial agreement

Different people independently select overlapping regions.

Level 5: Cross-person glyph agreement

They independently draw recognizably similar forms in those regions.

Level 6: Stimulus specificity

Reports change systematically when the image changes.

Level 7: Out-of-sample prediction

A map built from one group predicts where a new participant will report a form.

Level 8: Stable alphabet

Free drawings cluster into a reproducible set of glyph classes.

Level 9: Syntax

Glyph sequences display nonrandom ordering rules that generalize to new stimuli.

Level 10: Semantics

The glyphs reliably encode or predict independently verifiable information.

Level 11: Physical localization

The information is shown to arise from a particular external physical layer rather than display processing or shared neurobiology.

Level 12: “Code of reality”

Evidence establishes that the system is fundamental to the structure or operation of reality.

The public evidence currently concerns the first two levels. Goler explicitly identifies levels four and five as the unanswered questions the Vision Pro platform is intended to test.

A strong paragraph:

The project does not yet need to prove a simulation. It needs to prove the next rung: that one participant’s report predicts another participant’s report before the second person enters the experiment.

The gold-standard experiment

Phase 1: Register the stimulus

Publish:

The exact source image.

Its unedited RAW file.

The final displayed file.

Pixel dimensions.

Bit depth.

Color profile.

Exposure metadata.

Processing history.

Cryptographic hashes.
Vision Pro model and visionOS version.
